fields.title: Localization and Data Geography
fields.keyTakeaway: Localization affects copies, logs, caches, subprocessors, and employee access—and employee access is violated most often.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: The requirement to store data in-country—what does it affect?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: [[data-localisation|Data localization]] looks like a database requirement, but it turns out to be a requirement for the entire chain: backups, analytics, support, AI provider. Underestimating this leads to formal compliance while actually being in violation.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: Localization affects seven places, and three are usually forgotten:
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: *Primary database.* Obvious. *Backups.* Often in another region for reliability—a direct contradiction. *Analytics storage.* A separate system, a separate geography. *Logs.* Contain personal data and are often stored with a third-party service. *CDN and caches.* Cached personal responses physically reside at points of presence. *Subprocessors.* Each with its own geography. *Employee access.* Viewing data from another country is considered a transfer in some jurisdictions.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: The last one is the least obvious and most frequent violation: a support team in another country views data, and that constitutes a cross-border transfer.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: What determines the cost of compliance:
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: *A completely separate installation*—expensive, but straightforward and verifiable. *Data-type separation*—personal data locally, everything else shared. Cheaper, harder to operate. *Anonymization before transfer*—removes part of the data from the scope of the requirement.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: The product decision—**which markets we serve.** A localization requirement in a market where we have three clients might not justify a separate installation, and the right answer is not to enter that market.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *Domashniy chain.* Requirement to store in-country. Covered by a separate installation under a corporate tier, as discussed in `DS3-N3`.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: *AI provider.* Processing region agreed via contract, as discussed in `AI3-N4-L1`.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: When auditing the chain for the separate installation, two gaps were found: backups went to another region by default, and logs were written to a shared service. Both were fixed, but they would have been caught during a client audit.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: Employee access: support is located in the same country, so the issue did not arise. Noted as a constraint—hiring support in another country will make it an issue.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Localization requirements change, and a product compliant today may not be compliant in a year. Tracking this is the legal team's responsibility, but architectural flexibility is a product decision.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Localization affects copies, logs, caches, subprocessors, and employee access—and employee access is violated most often.
